reading.intro: Max, Lena's friend from England, lives in Hamburg. On Sunday he does something strange: he gets up at half past four.
reading.photos[0].caption: Die Fischauktionshalle: Musik, Bier und Fischbrötchen um sechs Uhr morgens.
reading.photos[1].caption: Die Fähre 62 fährt über die Elbe. Sie kostet so viel wie ein Busticket.
reading.en: Max lives in Hamburg and works in an office. On Monday the day is normal: the alarm rings at seven. Max showers, drinks coffee and eats a roll. Then he rides his bike to work. He works from nine to five. In the evening he cooks pasta, listens to music and reads a book. At eleven he sleeps. · On Sunday everything is different. The alarm rings at half past four. Max takes the bus to the fish market. The market opens at five. It is dark, but there are already a thousand people. They buy fish, fruit and flowers. In the hall a band plays, and people drink beer. At six in the morning! · Max buys a fish roll and watches the ships. Then he takes the ferry across the Elbe. At nine he is home again. He sleeps till twelve. “The fish market,” says Max, “is my Sunday.”
reading.fact: The Hamburg Fischmarkt has opened every Sunday at five since 1703. The sellers shout, the band plays in the auction hall, and half the crowd has not been to bed yet.

grammar[0].blocks[1].blocks[1].text: *Ich wohne in Berlin* is I live, I’m living and I do live in Berlin. Never try to build “I am living” in German.
grammar[0].fact: *Moin* is Hamburg's hello, at any hour. It is not “morning”: it comes from the old word for good, so *Moin* at midnight is fine, and *Moin Moin* is already chatty.

grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Three that shrink
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: *nehmen*: du nimmst, er nimmt — double m, no h. *essen*: du isst, er isst. *lesen*: du liest, never liesst.
grammar[1].fact: *Feierabend* is the moment work ends, and the evening that follows. *Schönen Feierabend!* is what colleagues say at five, and the first beer after it is the *Feierabendbier*.
